query: Consider the following context: How to rationally design composition of alloys with desired properties has always been an open and challenging question, especially for high-entropy alloy (HEA) which has huge selections of composition due to the feature of multi-principal elements. Although great efforts have been made in the past decades, such as approaches based on thermo-kinetic analysis and simulations, strategies to quick determine the optimal HEA composition remain lacking. In that context, which method can be used for design intrinsically strong, ductile, and low-weight refractory HEA (RHEA) compositions, and why?

generation.hypothesis: An integrated high-throughput design method that couples machine learning (ML) screening with thermodynamic and kinetic simulations will accelerate the identification of RHEA compositions combining high strength, ductility, and low weight.
generation.material_initial_state: A broad compositional space of refractory elements (e.g., W, Mo, Nb, Ta, etc.) without pre-imposed phase constraints and with typical random solid-solution characteristics.
generation.intervention: Apply an ML-driven high-throughput screening framework, informed by thermodynamic models and simulation data, to quickly predict and narrow down candidate RHEA compositions with optimized trade-offs among strength, ductility, and density.
generation.conditions: Testing under both room temperature for initial ductility/strength evaluation and elevated temperatures to assess high-temperature mechanical stability; standard processing routes such as arc-melting and homogenization.
generation.structural_mediator: The stabilization of a disordered BCC solid-solution matrix with tunable lattice distortions and controlled precipitation (if desired) to mediate dislocation movement.
generation.mechanism: The method leverages ML to correlate composition-dependent descriptors (e.g., atomic size differences, mixing enthalpy, and entropy) with thermodynamic trends predicted by simulations. This quickly identifies compositions that, when synthesized, are expected to form a stable matrix with inherent strengthening from lattice distortions and tailored microstructures that avoid brittle phases.
generation.predicted_outcome: RHEA compositions proposed by the integrated method will demonstrate a superior combination of ultra-high strength, appreciable ductility, and reduced density relative to alloys designed via conventional, trial-and-error approaches.
generation.baseline: Current design strategies relying solely on thermodynamic/kinetic simulation or experimental iterations without ML integration.
generation.boundary: The approach may be limited by the scope of the training data and simulation reliability when expanding to novel refractory elements or processing routes; thus, efficacy might diminish if the alloy system falls outside the validated range.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of property improvements is uncertain until validated experimentally. Additionally, the predictive accuracy of the ML models is contingent on the quality and breadth of the input data.

falsification_experiment.design: Use the integrated ML-thermodynamic framework to predict several RHEA compositions. Synthesize the top candidate alloys via conventional metallurgy methods. Conduct standardized mechanical tests (tensile, hardness, ductility, and density measurements) at both room and elevated temperatures. Compare the experimental performance with both the ML predictions and with benchmark RHEAs produced via traditional design methods.
measurements: Tensile strength and yield strength at room and elevated temperatures
Phase analysis (XRD, microscopy) to confirm microstructural features
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimentally synthesized alloys do not exhibit a statistically significant enhancement (e.g., higher strength-ductility product and lower density) compared to those produced by conventional methods, or if the predicted phase stability is not observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Other names such as “compositionally complex alloys (CCAs)” has also been given to this class of alloy containing multiple phases [3] . Nevertheless, the alloy design strategy of HEA/CCA shows great promise for exploring new alloy systems. RHEA was first proposed by Senkov et al . [4] as an attempt to create new alloy systems for high temperature applications beyond superalloys. The fields of aerospace and fossil energy have benefited from decades of the development of Ni-base superalloys. However, to obtain further efficiency gains and environmental friendliness, developing new materials with inexpensive, light, and strong characteristics is required. Numerous efforts can be found in the development of novel ferritic superalloys containing a disordered body-centered-cubic (BCC) matrix with ordered B2 and/or L2 1 precipitates due to their good creep resistance at elevated temperatures and relatively lower densities [1] , [2] . However, these emerging precipitation-strengthened ferritic alloys still face some drawbacks, such as the low high-temperature strength and not lightweight, which limit their applications. To overcome these issues, new alloy-design strategies are required. Recently, the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) or multi-principal-element alloys (MPEAs) has revolutionized the traditional alloy-design strategy, using multi-principal components (≥5) instead of one or two key components [3] – [10] .
